about: Habit 4 subject pack, as data. Questions are exported from the student assessment (services/demo-livelife/demos/livelife-student/backend.py) and rubrics from lib/livelifeDemo/rubrics.ts: change those and re-export together. Patterns, interventions and parallel scenarios are drafts for expert review.
brief: LiveLife Education, Discovering the Leader in Me, Level 5, Habit 4: Think Win-Win, students aged 11 to 16. Keep to its three mindsets, courage and consideration, the Emotional Bank Account as a metaphor, promises, and the five-part Win-Win Agreement. Win-Win does not mean both people get their first choice.
upload_hint: K1 to K9: the option letter. S1 to S8: the student's own written answer.
extension_task: Draft a Win-Win Agreement for a real situation in your class, then check it for all five parts.

WW-NAMES.name: Mixes up the mindset names
WW-NAMES.belief: Win-Win, Win-Lose and Lose-Win are interchangeable names.
WW-NAMES.student: Say who gets what they need in each one before naming it.
WW-NAMES.teacher: Sort short situations into the three mindsets, asking who gets what they need each time.
WW-NAMES.exit_check: A friend always picks the film and you never say what you want. Name the mindset and say why.

WW-GIVE-IN.name: Treats Win-Win as one person giving in
WW-GIVE-IN.belief: Win-Win means I should just agree.
WW-GIVE-IN.student: Ask: did what matters to me get said too?
WW-GIVE-IN.teacher: Use the lesson's point that Win-Win does not mean both get their first choice; contrast giving in with looking for a third option.
WW-GIVE-IN.exit_check: Your friend wants to leave early and you do not. What would Win-Win look like? Why is giving in not the same?

WW-INSIST.name: Treats a good outcome as getting my way
WW-INSIST.belief: My idea matters more than the other person's.
WW-INSIST.student: Before deciding, say what the other person needs.
WW-INSIST.teacher: Use Courage and Consideration: keep the courage to speak and add consideration for the other person.
WW-INSIST.exit_check: Your group must pick one topic and you love yours. What do you say first?

WW-ONE-SIDED.name: Decides without asking what the other person needs
WW-ONE-SIDED.belief: One side's need is enough to decide.
WW-ONE-SIDED.student: Write one question that finds out what the other person needs.
WW-ONE-SIDED.teacher: Practise asking before proposing: each pair states both needs, then one option that serves both.
WW-ONE-SIDED.exit_check: Two teams want the hall at the same time. What do you ask before suggesting a plan?

WW-DISMISS.name: Responds without listening
WW-DISMISS.student: Say back what you heard, then ask one respectful question.
WW-DISMISS.teacher: Model acknowledging a view before sharing your own; pairs rehearse with a low-stakes disagreement.
WW-DISMISS.exit_check: Write one sentence that shows you heard a classmate you disagree with.

WW-AVOID.name: Avoids or hides a broken promise
WW-AVOID.belief: If I say nothing, trust is not affected.
WW-AVOID.student: Tell the person early, say what happened, agree a next step.
WW-AVOID.teacher: Use the Emotional Bank Account as a metaphor: telling early protects trust, hiding withdraws from it.
WW-AVOID.exit_check: You cannot finish your part by the agreed time. What do you do, and when?

WW-VAGUE.name: Makes a promise too general to check
WW-VAGUE.belief: Meaning well is the same as a clear commitment.
WW-VAGUE.student: Add when, with whom, and how you will know you did it.
WW-VAGUE.teacher: Rewrite broad promises like 'be nicer' into an action, a time and a check.
WW-VAGUE.exit_check: Rewrite 'I will be helpful' as a promise you could check this week.

WW-AGREEMENT.name: Treats an agreement as a general rule
WW-AGREEMENT.belief: An agreement is a rule or a promise, without clear parts.
WW-AGREEMENT.student: Check for all five parts before you finish.
WW-AGREEMENT.teacher: Build one agreement together using Desired Results, Guidelines, Resources, Accountability and Consequences.
WW-AGREEMENT.exit_check: You and a friend share a bicycle. Write the five parts of your agreement.

H4-PARTIAL.name: Partly shown
H4-PARTIAL.belief: On the right track; part of what the rubric looks for is missing.
H4-PARTIAL.student: Look at the rubric's next level and add the missing part.

probes.WW-NAMES: A student always lets others choose. Which mindset is that, and who is not getting what they need?
probes.WW-GIVE-IN: If you agree just to stop an argument, is that Win-Win? Why or why not?
probes.WW-INSIST: Your idea was not chosen. What would still make the result fair?
probes.WW-ONE-SIDED: What would you need to know from the other person before you decide?
probes.WW-DISMISS: A classmate disagrees with you. What is the first thing you would say?
probes.WW-AVOID: You realise you cannot keep a promise. Who do you tell, and when?
probes.WW-VAGUE: How would someone else know that you kept this promise?
probes.WW-AGREEMENT: What would your agreement say about what happens if someone does not do their part?

separating_probes.probe: When two friends disagree, who should change their mind, and why?
Name the mindset in 'my idea must be chosen'. Would you do it that way yourself?

INT-H4-NAMES.title: Telling the mindsets apart (lesson: h4-mindsets)
steps: Recap the three ways to handle a problem.
Sort situations into the three mindsets.
Say who gets what they need in each.

INT-H4-GIVE-IN.title: Win-Win is not giving in (lesson: h4-mindsets)
steps: Contrast giving in with looking for a third option.
Replay one scenario both ways.
Students write an option that considers both.

INT-H4-INSIST.title: Courage with consideration (lesson: h4-mindsets)
steps: Revisit courage and consideration.
Find what the other person needs in a scenario.
Rewrite a demand as a shared proposal.

INT-H4-ONE-SIDED.title: Ask before deciding (lesson: h4-mindsets)
steps: Each partner states what they need.
Write one respectful question.
Propose an option and check it with both.

INT-H4-DISMISS.title: Listening when you disagree (lesson: h4-mindsets)
steps: Model acknowledging before responding.
Pairs rehearse with a low-stakes disagreement.
Write a sentence that shows listening.

INT-H4-AVOID.title: Protecting trust when a promise slips (lesson: h4-promises)
steps: Use the Emotional Bank Account metaphor.
Compare telling early with hiding it.
Write what to say and when.

INT-H4-VAGUE.title: Promises you can check (lesson: h4-promises)
steps: Compare a broad promise with a specific one.
Add action, time and check.
Rewrite a promise of your own.

INT-H4-AGREEMENT.title: The five parts of an agreement (lesson: h4-agreements)
steps: Name the five parts.
Build one agreement together.
Check a sample agreement for missing parts.

INT-H4-PRACTICE.title: Reaching the next rubric level
steps: Read the next rubric level.
Add the missing part to your own answer.

options.A: I get what I want even if you do not.
options.B: I give up what I want every time.
options.C: We look for a solution that considers what matters to both of us.

items.text: I insist on choosing the game and my friend cannot choose. Which mindset does this most closely show?
Your partner wants quiet to work, while you want to discuss ideas aloud. What is the best first step?

options.C: Ask what they need and share what you need.

items.text: Both classmates want to use the same materials at the same time. Which is a possible Win-Win option?

options.C: Plan turns or divide materials based on the task.

items.text: What is a helpful way to respond when a classmate explains their point of view?

options.B: Listen and ask a respectful question.

items.text: You promised to bring a game but realize you cannot. What is the responsible action?

options.C: Tell the person early, explain briefly and agree on a next step.

items.text: Which list contains the five parts of a Win-Win Agreement?

options.A: Desired Results, Guidelines, Resources, Accountability, Consequences.

items.text: Which is the most useful promise?

options.C: During tomorrow’s group task, I will listen to each partner before suggesting an idea.

items.text: Every break, you let your friend choose the game because you do not want an argument, even when you would like a turn. Which mindset does this most closely show?
Two friends disagree about whether to play football or a board game. One student says, “Win-Win means I should just agree with my friend.” What would you suggest they do?

rubric.indicators: Strong answer: clarify that Win-Win is not always giving in; both should share what matters and look for an option considering both (e.g., play one now and schedule the other, if both agree).
rubric.levels_text: 4: Correctly explains Win-Win is not giving in and proposes a fair option considering both. 3: Accurate explanation plus a relevant next step. 2: Says “take turns/compromise” but does not clarify the misconception or needs. 1: Recommends one person always giving in or one person winning. 0: Blank, unrelated or disrespectful/shaming.
elements: explains Win-Win is not just giving in
proposes a fair option that considers both friends

retest: Two cousins disagree about which show to watch. One says, “Win-Win means I just have to let you pick.” What would you suggest?
Your group disagrees about where to sit. Someone says, “Fine, I’ll give up, that’s Win-Win.” What would you say?
practice: Two friends want different snacks to share. What would a Win-Win look like?
A friend says Win-Win means nobody gets anything they want. What would you tell them?

items.text: During a class vote, a student says, “My idea must be chosen; other ideas do not matter.” Which mindset is shown? Explain briefly and suggest a better approach.

rubric.indicators: Strong answer: identifies Win-Lose; proposes hearing ideas and selecting/combining an option that considers the group’s needs.
rubric.levels_text: 4: Correctly identifies Win-Lose, explains why, and suggests inclusive alternative. 3: Correct classification and suitable alternative; explanation limited. 2: Classification or alternative is right, but not both. 1: Misclassifies or endorses domination. 0: Blank/irrelevant/harmful.

retest: A team captain says, “We do it my way or not at all.” Which mindset is this? Explain and suggest a better approach.
A student always stays quiet and lets others decide, even when upset. Which mindset is this? Suggest a better approach.
practice: Someone says, “If I win, you have to lose.” Which mindset is this, and why?
A friend says, “Whatever you want, I don’t matter.” Which mindset is this, and what could help?

items.text: Your teammate wants more time to practice; you want to finish the project today. What would you ask or say before deciding?

rubric.indicators: Strong answer: asks what practice is needed and shares own deadline concern; listens and explores a plan that addresses both.
rubric.levels_text: 4: Clearly acknowledges both needs and uses respectful questions to explore. 3: Recognizes both perspectives and asks a useful question. 2: Mentions one side or gives a vague “talk about it.” 1: Dismisses the other person’s need. 0: Blank/irrelevant/shaming.
elements: asks a respectful question to explore
shows listening or exploring a plan for both

retest: Your friend wants to revise tonight; you want to go out. What would you ask or say before deciding?
Your partner wants to present first; you are nervous about going last. What would you say before deciding?
practice: A teammate wants a bright poster and you want a simple one. What would you ask them?
Your sibling wants the room quiet and you want music. What would you ask first?

items.text: Two students need the same computer for different parts of a project. Suggest one solution that could work for both and say how you would check it is fair.

rubric.indicators: Strong answer: proposes a feasible schedule/turns or shared plan; checks each student’s agreement and task needs.
rubric.levels_text: 4: Feasible solution addresses both needs and explicitly checks mutual acceptance/fairness. 3: Practical solution that considers both; check may be implicit. 2: Possible solution but one need or fairness check omitted. 1: Gives computer to one person without consideration. 0: Blank/irrelevant/harmful.
elements: proposes a feasible solution for both students

retest: Two classmates need the same library book this week. Suggest one solution and say how you would check it is fair.
Two groups want the same practice ground after school. Suggest one solution and how you would check it is fair.
practice: Two friends need the same calculator for a test and homework. What could work for both?
Two students both want the window seat on a trip. What could work for both?

items.text: In a discussion, your classmate says something you disagree with. Write one sentence you could say that shows listening and respect.

rubric.indicators: Strong answer example: “I hear that you think ____. Can you tell me why? I see it differently because ____.”
rubric.levels_text: 4: Respectful acknowledgement plus open question or calm sharing of own view. 3: Respectful response with either acknowledgement or constructive question. 2: Polite but generic, with little listening evidence. 1: Interrupting, insulting or dismissive language. 0: Blank or abusive response.
elements: respectfully acknowledges what the classmate said
asks an open question or calmly shares own view

retest: A classmate says your favourite sport is boring. Write one sentence that shows listening and respect.
In a debate, a classmate challenges your point. Write one sentence you could say that shows respect.
practice: A friend thinks your plan will not work. What could you say first?
Someone in your group has a different answer from yours. What could you say?

items.text: You promised your sibling/friend you would help, but you cannot do it at the agreed time. What would you do to protect trust?

rubric.indicators: Strong answer: communicates early and honestly, acknowledges promise, and offers a realistic agreed alternative/next step.
rubric.levels_text: 4: Timely honest communication, ownership, and realistic mutually agreed repair. 3: Communicates honestly and suggests a next step. 2: Says apologize but lacks timing/plan. 1: Avoids, blames or hides. 0: Blank/irrelevant or endorses dishonesty.
elements: offers a realistic next step or agreed repair

retest: You told a friend you would return their notes today, but you left them at home. What would you do to protect trust?
You agreed to help with a poster but have a family event. What would you do to protect trust?
practice: You will be late to meet a friend. What would you do?
You forgot to do your part of a group task. What would you do next?

items.text: You and a classmate want to share a game console. What would you include in your agreement so it is clear and fair?

rubric.indicators: Strong answer should include: Desired Results (both get fair play time); Guidelines (turn length/order); Resources (console/controllers/time); Accountability (timer/checklist/partner check); Consequences (fair, related agreed next step if plan is not followed).
rubric.levels_text: 4: Addresses all five components accurately with specific fair terms. 3: Correctly addresses 4 components and agreement is workable. 2: Includes 2–3 components or mostly vague terms. 1: Only general promise/rule; most components absent. 0: Blank or proposes punitive, humiliating or unrelated consequence.

retest: You and a neighbour want to share a cricket bat. What would you include in your agreement so it is clear and fair?
You and your sibling want to share a tablet. What would you include in your agreement so it is clear and fair?
practice: Your group is sharing art supplies. What should your agreement include?
Two friends are planning to share chores for a class party. What should their agreement include?

items.text: Choose one situation in which you could practice Think Win-Win this week. What specific action will you take, and how will you check whether you kept your promise?

rubric.indicators: Strong answer: names a realistic situation; describes observable action; identifies simple check-in/evidence (self-check, partner reminder, completed plan).
rubric.levels_text: 4: Situation, specific observable action and supportive accountability/check all present. 3: Specific action and context; check is less clear. 2: Goal is relevant but broad (“be nicer”) or lacks evidence/check. 1: Unrealistic, externally imposed or not linked to Think Win-Win. 0: Blank/irrelevant/shaming.
elements: says how they will check they kept the promise

retest: Choose one situation at home where you could practise Think Win-Win this week. What will you do, and how will you check?
Choose one group activity at school this week. What specific action will you take, and how will you check?
practice: Write one Win-Win action for tomorrow and how you will know you did it.
Write one promise for this week that someone else could check.
